speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) in connection with the important mission to London from which he has just returned, I wish to make some comments in connection with this and other matters relating to the present foreign situation.
Whatever may be said in a debate such as this, I think the first words of members on this side of the House of Commons ought to be to the effect that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke in London and took the stand he did with respect to the North Atlantic council decisions he spoke not merely for the government but also for parliament and for the nation, and that parliament and the nation will give him wholehearted and unanimous support in that stand.
I suppose it will be only natural for members of this house who have sat here for a number of years to recall the conditions of previous years and reflect upon the extent to which our foreign policy objectives have slowly but surely made an almost complete

turn from isolation to full-blown co-operation in world affairs. It is a far cry from the day some fifteen years ago when this house heard declarations by virtue of which this country made a hasty retreat from international co-operation in connection with the oil sanctions having to do with the Abyssinian issue. It is a far cry, too, from the days when, just prior to world war II, the government-and the people were perhaps largely behind them-said that they were proud of the fact that this country had no international commitments of any kind whatsoever. It is also a far cry from those days when we were just on the threshold of world war II, and when we debated in this house the problem of Canada's remaining neutral in the event of a world-wide conflagration. But fortunately for our people and for this parliament, those days have gone; and the decisions of the North Atlantic council, which have been so well described by the minister this afternoon, have seen Canada and her friends of the north Atlantic community now going the whole way in burning the last vestige of the bridges of isolation for this country.
The defence of the north Atlantic community is now to be shared by the twelve nations which are signatories to that pact. We had already been committed on principle to that very thing, but this last council meeting did far more than that. It put flesh upon the dry bones of the original pact, and, as a first step, it has translated that principle into the first stages of action. We are now to have, as the minister described it, a specialization with respect to our defence, and balanced collective forces with the minimum of duplication of effort within the north Atlantic community. In other words, each partner is to do what it is best equipped and fitted to do.
Up until now the fulfilment of our commitments under the North Atlantic pact was largely predicated upon one of the signatory powers being the victim of an aggressor. We have now gone the next step forward and have made that commitment applicable before any aggression has taken place. I think it will be evident to everyone in this house that, with this further step forward, when t-his integration of our armed1 and economic effort has been effected, we shall have committed ourselves to the policy that we shall not-nor shall any of the nations in the north Atlantic community-any longer follow a go-it-alone policy. Conversely, the collective obligation which we have now assumed to help a nation that is invaded becomes that much stronger. We are now in a community chain, and each link in that
External Affairs
chain becomes much more important than it ever was before; because if one link of the integrated defence or economic forces is broken, of course the whole chain itself becomes gravely weakened. In other words, we have joined in a common policy for the defence of the north Atlantic area.
I think all of us had an additional concern in our minds as the minister and the communiques from time to time brought to the people of this country the message as to what was done at London. We all remember that prior to the last world war great stress was laid upon the alleged impregnability of the then powerful Maginot line. We saw that Maginot line circumvented. We saw it made useless as a defence against aggression. One of the things we have to watch for and to concern ourselves with now is that in this north Atlantic community arrangement, this integrated defence arrangement and plan, we are not isolating our north Atlantic community and are not failing to lay sufficient emphasis upon other parts of the world scene, which parts might easily prove to be the soft underbelly of our whole defence structure, whereby Soviet imperialism might readily avoid striking the strong Maginot line of north Atlantic defence, swing around and outflank us in southeast Asia and other vulnerable areas. We must see to it that the back door to Asia is not left open. I was glad to hear the minister state that there would be a further report forthcoming with respect to the Canberra talks, from which the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) has just returned. I was glad, too, that the Big Three ministers, meeting, as they did, almost concurrently with the north Atlantic council, placed considerable emphasis upon the situation in southeast Asia.
After all, Russian objectives perhaps are not so much pointed at the moment at the stone wall of the north Atlantic defences as they are toward southeast Asia-yes, and toward Japan. The reasons are of course clear to all; because were they to be successful in concentrating their immediate endeavours and their attack on that part of the world, it would mean that not only would key strategic positions be lost to the democratic cause, but there would be a loss of important sources of raw materials in that part of the world, with all the attendant dangers flowing from such a loss.
The loss of Burma, Thailand and Indochina, and the outflanking of Japan, Okinawa and the Philippines, would leave these latter areas strategically, economically and politically in a position of almost untenability. It needs no stretch of the imagination to see the

External Affairs
position in which our good friends of Pakistan and India, who are not yet self-sufficient in the matter of food, would be placed were such a successful flanking movement to take place.
I am most anxious that while we are balancing our economic and military defences in the north Atlantic community we shall not allow ourselves to become isolated, only to find that the flanking movement around that great economic and defence "Maginot" line has struck in softer and more vulnerable spots. We should, so far as possible, lay as much emphasis as we can upon trying to stop the aggression which is so obviously taking place in southeast Asia, and which, were it carried to the conclusion one can visualize, might easily weaken the structure of the north Atlantic community itself.
I know the people and parliament of Canada will support the government in its practical and realistic efforts to enforce peace against any dangerous combination which understands only the language of force and power. I sat in this House of Commons years ago and heard members from time to time- and they were honest, sincere and patriotic members-offer the considered opinion, which was shared by a great many people in Canada, that if this or any other country attempted to prepare for war, somehow or other it was taking a step toward war and away from peace. How often we heard the statement made-and it was accepted in many parts of the country-that if we manufacture weapons and train men, those weapons and men will be turned against some enemy, and in such endeavours we would be moving toward war.
The period in between the two great wars saw us taking that principle to heart, but the unpreparedness of those days did not bring peace; it brought war. It might not have been the only reason for the war, but in any event it is sufficient to show all of us that our being unprepared did not stop aggression, did not stop the holocaust of a second world war. I believe therefore that the people of Canada are ready to try another principle, are ready to see if we cannot enforce peace and make those who would break the peace keep it by being sufficiently strong to avert attack at any time.
In this tough world, where tough and realistic men are anxious to achieve world domination, we must meet fire with fire. As General Eisenhower in effect said, not long ago in an address at Columbia university, unpreparedness, in the condition in which the world now finds itself, is just as criminal as war itself. I am quite sure that when a few

moments ago the minister, on behalf of a peace-loving people, voiced the government's aims in connection with the north Atlantic community, said that it was driving toward peace as the chief objective, he said what the people of Canada wanted to hear. The people of this country do not want preparations for war; they want preparations which will ensure peace rather than have world casualty lists published for a third time.
It is the hope of all members of the north Atlantic community that the realistic movement now being made toward peace may lead to a permanent, just and lasting peace. In return for the support that parliament and the people of Canada will give the government, perhaps in a measure greater than it could have expected, parliament and the people will expect the government to tell the whole unvarnished story with respect to the position in which we find ourselves under these new north Atlantic arrangements. In view of the support thus given, the country is entitled to as much information as can be made public, having in mind security considerations. Canadians can take whatever message in this respect there may be, and will be prepared to shoulder whatever burdens the alliance of the north Atlantic community may involve.
However, having said that Canadians can take it, one must add at once that they should know exactly what the future holds for them on all political fronts. They would like to know whether, in the opinion of the government and those closely associated with it in diplomatic affairs, this means that we are moving closer to peace than to war. They would like to know if this is a step, even though a short and halting one, toward a full-blown north Atlantic political and economic federation.
A few moments ago the minister used the word "commonwealth" in describing the movement of the north Atlantic community. Perhaps this gives more point to the question I have just asked. Do the present activities of the north Atlantic community imply-and I believe the people are entitled to know this-that, one day, through the various steps taken, there will be only an Atlantic army, navy and air force, having in mind the integrating features of the plan just placed before parliament and the people? While in a matter of this kind costs are perhaps a secondary or tertiary consideration, the people of Canada ought to be told what additional cost is involved. After all, if we have to tighten our belts, we ought to know how far we have to tighten them. It is only a matter of information. Whatever may be the cost of peace,

it can never equal the tragic cost of war. I think the Canadian people are ready to assume their full burden. Secretary of State Acheson, informally addressing a meeting of the congress of the United States, indicated in general terms what the United States people would have to face by way of heavier burdens. Our people ought to know that too. It is part and parcel of the information which the government ought to give our public today.
After all, the government may not be able to take the public into its confidence on all military matters that may be involved, but it ought to take the public into its confidence as to how much it expects of them.
The next question I should like to have answered is this: What part in the economic defence plans will Canada play so far as security is concerned? I know the minister was hesitant about that, for reasons which I think were proper; but I hope that as soon as that information can be given, it will be given, subject to security considerations, to parliament and to the Canadian people. In other words, the Canadian people ought to be told the full implications of this new policy of balanced collective defence; because there is no better way of securing and maintaining the unanimous support of the public of Canada, common-sense and responsible citizens that they are, than to tell them the full facts. When they have the full facts, the Canadian people never let their leaders down.
I should like to make one reference, if I may, to the concurrent meetings of the north Atlantic council and the foreign ministers of the United States, Great Britain and France. I think it was fortunate that those meetings were held at the same time, because, as the minister pointed out a few minutes ago, they helped to clarify the situation with respect' to economic considerations affecting their respective countries and their relationships with those parts of the north Atlantic community that are in Europe. However, for those in the house who might wish to refresh their memories with respect to what was agreed to by this country in connection with the economic and social aspects of the North Atlantic pact, I should like to read into the record article 2, which reads as follows:
The parties will contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions, by bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stability and wellbeing. They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
External Affairs
It has been pointed out by many statesmen of the world that you cannot separate peace from prosperity; they are indivisible. For that reason there is an economic part of the North Atlantic pact which is indivisible in respect to this country. While perhaps in the early meetings the question of military aid had to be emphasized, still I think that Canada, the third trading nation of the world, whose economic prosperity depends upon the economic health of the world at large, realizes that article 2 becomes a vital and important part of the North Atlantic pact.
I summon as a witness to my argument with respect to the economic aspects of the quest for peace the words which were uttered within the hearing of all of us in this chamber the other day by the Prime Minister of Pakistan, who said:
But democracy, In Pakistan or elsewhere, Is of little use to the common man unless its advantages are made available to him in his daily life and his standard of living is raised at least to a level which gives him a substantial stake in the way of life which he has chosen for himself.
Then he went on to say:
. . . for there can be no progress without peace, no peace without progress and the removal of the economic disequilibrium, so apparent in Asia, which keeps more than half the world in poverty and the ferment of discontent, or without international co-operation, which we believe to be the greatest need of all countries, great and small.
Another great and powerful statesman, Prime Minister Nehru of India, spoke in this chamber last fall and uttered words just as strong in support of that argument. The economic and social life of the world is bound up in this whole question of striving toward peace in our time. When these matters of defence are being discussed by the deputies, our choice of a permanent deputy for Canada will have been of great importance, because he will have to deal not only with defence problems, but with the equally important problems of the economics upon which the prosperity of this country is so completely predicated.
In connection with the military and economic defence measures that are to be taken, I should like the minister to tell us at a convenient time whether civilian defence was considered at that meeting. The minister pointed out that while civilians were in the front line in the last war, they are going to be in a much more dangerous position in the next war if there is one. I am afraid that civilian defence is quite often overlooked or relegated to the background in our consideration of defence matters. I submit that it should be placed further up in the priority rating, because, after all, safety and security from outside aggression, whether in other

External Affairs
countries or in our own, are of prime importance to the people of Canada as a whole.
I think it is important to realize just how much alarmed the people on the other side of the border are with respect to the matter of civilian defence. I have in my hand the current issue of the United States News and World Report, which in one paragraph gives an example of just how much alarmed they may be over there. This is one of the statements made:
Key industries-
This is, in the United States.
-will have to be put 100 feet underground if they are to be assured of protection from the hydrogen bomb that scientists consider a coming weapon. W. Stuart Symington, new head of the national security resources board, is trying to decide how to break the bad news to the public about what civilian defence will cost in preparing against war involving atomic weapons. Idea until now has been to play down the need for vast new programs costing untold millions to provide the public with the protection it would want in another war.
I point that out as one indication of how those in another part of the world feel with respect to this matter.
I also want to ask the minister, if there was any discussion with respect to civilian defence, whether civilian defence formed a part of the integrated defence program of the north Atlantic community. In some places the prospective costs of civilian defence so far as individual nations are concerned may very well be such that they ought to be pooled in the interests of an integrated and balanced collective defence system. I do not mind saying, Mr. Speaker, and I think I reflect the views of many, that, from the information parliament has, Canada is alarmingly and dangerously behind in her plans for civilian defence for the safety and security of our citizens in case of some unwanted eventuality of the future. I should also like to ask the minister if he will indicate at the proper time whether there was any formal or informal discussion while he was in London, of the vexed question of the recognition of the Chinese Red government. Secretary of state Acheson, in answer to one of the questions propounded to him at the unofficial meeting of congress the other day, indicated that there was .some slight sliding from the original position which the United States took as to the recognition of the Chinese Red government. He indicated that the United States government were not now prepared to support its entry into the United Nations, or to give it that much recognition, but that they would not veto such a proposal. Perhaps the minister will enlighten us, at -a convenient time, as to what changes have taken place in that position during the last few weeks.
[Mr. Graydon.l
I want to come now to another point having to do With our relations with our great and friendly neighbour to the south. In that regard the minister clarified our position in what I thought was an admirable speech he made in London, a speech which was favourably commented upon by many newspapers. Parliament will support him in what he said on that occasion. Nevertheless certain proposals have been made by persons who perhaps carry some weight in the business world of the United States, and perhaps a private member of the house may be pardoned for making certain observations about them at this time. In doing so I want to indicate clearly that I think a nation that has reached maturity in world affairs should avoid, as I am going to try to avoid, the temptation of barking at every wagon that goes by in the international show. Nevertheless I think most Canadians were calmly amused at an article which appears in the current issue of a magazine called Look which is published in the United States. The article was written by George E. Shea, Jr., financial editor of the Wall Street Journal. I am not going to attempt to read the whole article, because it is lengthy. The heading of the article is, "Why the United States and Canada should be one country". In the article he says:
The frontier between Canada and the United States is becoming today an oppressive cord that threatens to strangle the progress and security of both our countries. Dating back to the revolutionary war, the border for many years has meant little more than an inconvenience. People may have thought idly that it made little sense. But they have put up with it as one submits to any senseless but harmless routine. Now, however, the arbitrary division of the continent is beginning to hurt both countries in two fundamental ways: (1) it is serving to hold back the development of Canada's wealth; and, as our natural resources are gradually exhausted it is also restricting United States economic welfare; (2) it is weakening the .ability of the two countries to ensure the military security of the continent in an age of new intercontinental weapons. The time has come to think seriously of making the United States and Canada one country or, to start with, at least one economic unit.
First of all I want to say most sincerely to the author and to the magazine in question that we are very grateful for the highly complimentary things the author said about Canada. We regard it as a very high compliment that a nation as great as the United States should consider a marriage with us, even though it may be a marriage of convenience, with a rather substantial marriage settlement or dowry attached to it; because the author goes on to make one reference that I thought was interesting. He said:
How senseless the frontier is has been pointed up sharply with the recent news of Canada's fabulous oil bonanza in Alberta.

If our point of view would be helpful to the average United States citizen, then perhaps it ought to be stated. I should like to say to the author of the article and to the American people: You are our good and friendly neighbours. Let anyone in the world say anything against you and Canada will rise to your defence. We like you and admire you. We find it easy to work with you. Our nations provide a compelling example of how two nations, one small and one large, can make peaceful relations permanent. You are doing all right, and so are we. Please do not embarrass us with this latest proposal for national marriage. No matter how highly we feel complimented by the offer, we are sorry; we cannot accept the ring.
In addition I want to echo the well chosen words that the minister used in London as to this very point. I think they provide a complete answer. This is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in London, as reported in the Times:
In this central theme of his speech, Mr. Pearson carried on the thought of his previous speech to the Pilgrims, when he spoke of Canada as the little fellow between two giants. Canadians, he said, had a special part to play in the world because they were "bilingual, not merely in the French-English sense, but in the sense that we speak English and American." Canada is a North American nation, living an American life and thinking American thought; yet at the same time extremely content and wholehearted in her membership of the British commonwealth.
Mr. Pearson was at pains to reassure his audience that his country was not passing through a transitional stage towards becoming a United States satellite; but in thinking they needed any such assurance he was unnecessarily modest. The time is long past when Englishmen could think of Canada as capable of becoming the satellite of anybody.
Now I want to pass to another point, and say to those who were responsible for the article from which I have just read that we might be talking about other and less romantic things than a national marriage between the United States and Canada. There is the question of the renewal of the Hyde Park agreement in some modernized and modified form. Perhaps in that respect I should quote the opinion of some Americans themselves, as it appeared in the current issue of Newsweek. This writer, dealing with Canadian affairs, spoke of this very thing:
As Pearson prepared to give the Commons a fuller explanation of what Canada got itself into at London, a big question was what military contribution Canada could make. The United States-Canada joint defence program had been a onesided affair so far, with Canada using up scarce dollars to buy American parts and equipment. The first Canadian arms sale to the United States since the war will be made in the fiscal year beginning July 1. Purchases between $15 million and $25 million will offset approximately the amount of dominion arms buying in the United States.
External Affairs
Buying and selling: It is not known what Canadian items will be sold. The best guess is medium artillery and special equipment for Arctic warfare. The defence department thinks there is no chance of the United States taking the CF-100, the long-range all-weather Avro jet fighter, which Canada desperately wants to sell.
The arms deal represents a modification of the "Buy American Act" which had been construed to prevent such purchases. This removes a longstanding issue between the two countries. Canadians had complained that they had to spend their precious dollars for American military equipment, while the United States always found some excuse for not buying Canadian-made equipment.
That temporary solution is all right as far as it goes, but I should think there is a very great need for a permanent revival of the-Hyde Park agreement in some modernized form. I am particularly interested in this, in common with many others who are so very proud of the CF-100, which is manufactured at Malton in the county of Peel, which I represent. Both the management and the workmen who have had to do with the production of that great aircraft take pride in its achievements, and we are hopeful that in time it will find a market in the country to the south.
In my concluding remarks on this matter I should like to deal with the economic aspects of our north Atlantic position as they concern our domestic affairs here at home, because they are interrelated and vital to the success of the pact itself. Although full details of the obligations are not yet known, it is becoming evident that the economic aspects of the Atlantic pact are and will continue to be very much to the forefront in the days that lie ahead, as I was attempting to indicate previously. The Prime Minister foresaw this aspect of the developments as far back as-1948, when the idea of the North Atlantic pact was crystallizing in the minds of government leaders, both in Europe and on this continent. As evidence of this, the Prime Minister's radio speech to the Canadian people on November 11, 1948, called upon us to support the North Atlantic pact. In that speech, obviously with the economic aspects in view, the Prime Minister stated that it was the opinion of the Canadian government at that time that a security treaty such as was proposed could not be fully effective if it was nothing more than a military alliance; and with that I think this parliament agrees. Fifteen days later the Secretary of State for External Affairs, at a press conference at The Hague, stated that Canada would commit herself freely to military measures specific enough for security.
While full details of the obligations of the-signatory powers are not yet public, it is evident that as a nation we have made our commitment from the military point of view" and from the size of the estimates for national

External Affairs
defence this year in Canada we are moving toward carrying out these commitments. There is little evidence, and certainly there has been no announced government policy, as to the other and equally important aspects of our responsibilities under this pact, namely the economic aspects, and what we are doing, and more important what we propose to do, in the way of development of our resources to meet the demands that will fall upon this nation in fulfilling our obligations under this pact.
Perhaps before we entered into a balanced, integrated defence policy under the pact there was not the compelling pressure upon us to develop our own natural resources that there is at the present time, though I believe we should have been doing something along that line in preparation for what looked like an obvious eventuality. This aspect of responsibility is equally important in respect to any military measures pledged by this nation, first because it is the sphere of co-operation from which the greatest assistance may rightfully be expected from Canada, and second, because it is the determining factor upon which the extent of the military measures which can be sustained by this nation must necessarily be determined.
As a nation of only fourteen million people we cannot be expected to contribute anything like the numbers of men that could be supplied by some of our allies in the Atlantic pact. What we lack in available manpower, however, because of our population, we more than make up in agricultural, industrial and natural resources, of the very kind any gigantic defence program in modern warfare must have if its efforts are to 'be sustained and successful. In the last war the contribution made by this nation in material resources, so essential to the success of our own forces and those of our allies, exceeded all expectations. Today the challenge to the defence preparedness of this nation by virtue of our obligations under the Atlantic pact and the ever-present challenge of world domination by communism makes our marvellous contribution in the past pale into insignificance. The demands upon Canada in this particular field will be even greater than ever before in our history.
There is growing evidence that the economic resources of the United States, partic-cularly in the field of raw materials essential to any continental defence preparedness program, are showing signs of becoming exhausted. Considered in the light of expected demands in accordance with obligations under the Atlantic pact, the result is alarming. The most recent issue of the same United States publication from which I quoted just a few moments ago, Look, has
[Mr. Graydon.l
this to say as to why the United States and Canada should be one country. I quote this paragraph:
The United States suffers just as much from the frontier. We are losing out especially today because we are turning from a "have" nation into a "have-not" nation.
Whereas we used to ship oil, copper, zinc and lead to the rest of the world, we now have begun to import all of these essential materials. And the proportion of imports in every case seems sure to grow. The same thing is happening in iron ore and timber. We used to be able to produce more of these things than we could possibly use. Now we use more than we can possibly produce.
Then the article goes on to mention other matters with which I shall not weary the house at this stage of my argument; but the main argument is based on the fact that Canada has the natural resources but not the development, while the natural resources of the United States are becoming depleted. We cannot continue to be unmindful of the fact that our failure to develop our natural resources is a source of wonderment to others, even to our most friendly neighbours.
Nor is this assertion of failure to develop our resources to the point Where it may be considered as at least equal to our obligations, first for our defence and second under the Atlantic pact, confined to sources outside of Canada. I should like to quote an inside source as well.
Only recently, General Howard, the general manager of the Canadian Industrial Preparedness Association, said this in Ottawa, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of March 30, 1950:
"There is too much thinking of preparedness in terms of men, arms and munitions when we should be considering how many tons of steel, rubber, lead, tin and even paint we need," Major General C. B. Howard, C.B.E., of Montreal, said in Ottawa yesterday.
Speaking on "Canadian industrial preparedness" to a luncheon meeting of the Ottawa branch of the Naval Officers Association of Canada, General Howard, who is general manager of the Canadian Industrial Preparedness Association, said the navy, army and air force were only parts of a plan of defence. Research and industry, he asserted, were equally important in the defence plans of this country.
He went on to outline eight points of a plan for complete mobilization of Canada's material and industrial resources. Some of these might fit in more particularly now, in view of our integrated scheme for 'collective defence. These were his points:
1.	Complete mobilization of industrial resources.
2.	Efficient and effective attention to distribution and employment of manpower in the armed services and in industry.
3.	Mobilization of Canada's financial resources with mutually satisfactory financial arrangements.
4.	Distribution to industry of designs and data on all designs not in normal course of production.

5.	Adequate and authoritative inspection of design branches to avoid duplication and production of certain items.
6.	Storage and distribution arrangements to the armed forces.
7.	Supply and storage of materials in short supply.
8.	Shadow government department or departments to deal with problems of supply and priorities.
Some of us might be inclined to disagree with some of these proposals, but I mention them all to point up one of the important things about which I am in agreement with General Howard, and that is the importance of developing our natural resources, in view of our extended obligations under the North Atlantic pact.
Unfortunately parliament and the country at large are not in a position to judge accurately whether or not our efforts to develop the resources of this country are adequate under the circumstances, because neither this parliament nor the country has been told the full extent of Canada's obligations under the Atlantic pact. There are, however, grave doubts in the minds of many people, both within and without the boundaries of Canada, as to the adequacy of the development of our resources to meet the demands which would fall upon this nation should the day ever come when the signatory nations to the Atlantic pact find it necessary to defend themselves against aggression. True, our annual defence costs today are not far short of the total ordinary expenditure of the federal government before the last war. True, there must be strict avoidance of panicky overspending, and the taxpayer must be assured that every dollar spent in our defence, whether direct or within our obligations under the Atlantic pact, be spent to the best advantage.
But the Canadian people want some assurance from the government that our resources are being directed into the most profitable channels and in a manner that will assure an adequate defence program; that will make it possible for this nation to carry out its obligations under the Atlantic pact, in the sphere of activity where we can make our best and most valuable contribution. The people also want some assurance from the government that present plans for the development of the resources of this country are sufficient to meet the demands we may expect in this sphere, as a result of the recent decision of the Atlantic treaty conference. Recently press dispatches reported that the Atlantic treaty nations had agreed, by united efforts, to build up a system of defence capable of withstanding any external threat directed against any of them. As a result of this decision, Canada as a nation stands obligated to come to the rescue not only of
External Affairs
any signatory nation that is attacked, but to the defence of Europe, under the obligation to build by united efforts with the countries of western Europe "a unified system of defence." This means that our obligations up until now were projected into the future, dependent upon one of the signatory powers being attacked. Today, as a result of this recent decision of the Atlantic treaty council, our obligations are now due. Carrying out these commitments involves the economic phase of our obligations. The second decision, having to do with the creation of balanced collective forces, involves the question of trained manpower, and directly concerns the Department of National Defence.
With regard to our commitments under the economic aspect of our obligations under the Atlantic pact, however, the minister of external affairs should give some indication to parliament and the country just what program the government has in mind. While there may be some justification for secrecy with regard to efforts directed to meet obligations under the collective forces commitment, no such reason exists for secrecy as to plans for the development of the resources of this country and our industrial and agricultural potential.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to conclude by saying that this is a critical stage in the life of a young, progressive, peace-seeking nation such as ours. It calls for calm fortitude, national unity, and prayerful determination on the part of our people. It calls for the best and most constructive statesmanship parliament can apply. Let us resolve to march as one toward that goal of permanent peace upon which the welfare, happiness, and survival of our peoples are so completely predicated.

subsubtopic: ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE TO SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ASIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we heard from the minister a statement which was interesting, concise and important. I very much regret that it was delivered before a house so sparsely filled. This was due not so much to lack of interest as to pressure of other affairs. This morning we had an important debate on agriculture. Many of the members who were interested in the problem before the house were unable to be present and participate. This afternoon the social security committee, as well as other committees, is sitting. It is unfortunate that this debate is held under these circumstances.
I must say I appreciated the minister's statement this afternoon, and I shall look forward with a great deal of interest to the report to he made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) with regard to the Sydney conference. He will place more fully before

External Affairs
the house the discussions with regard to southeast Asia, and the manner in which we can assist the people of that area in building up their economy and their resistance to the threat of totalitarianism. When I speak of "totalitarianism", I am thinking not only of totalitarianism in the communistic form but totalitarianism which does exist, and indeed may extend to some other part of Asia, owing to the reinstatement of other reactionary regimes such as once held sway in those countries. I often think that the democratic powers have been placed in a difficult position with regard to Asia Minor and Asia in that, from time to time, the force of events has compelled them to assist regimes that were anything but democratic or which [DOT]did not conform in any respect to our democratic viewpoint. I shall therefore be interested in hearing what the Minister of .Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) has to say about the Sydney conference and the aid to southeast Asia.
I was glad to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) say that, on his visit to the United Kingdom, he found that both in the United Kingdom and in western Europe there was a new spirit of optimism and that conditions evidently were improving in that area. I think perhaps he is right when he says this is due largely to Marshall aid and perhaps to a greater feeling of security because of the North Atlantic agreement. But, after all, the strengthening of the economies of the western European countries and, indeed, of the economies of the nations throughout the world, is our best assurance against the outbreak of another war. We of this party will continue to give every support to, and to exert every influence we can on, shaping a Canadian international policy directed toward ending the cold war and endeavouring to find a secure basis for future peace. As has been stressed this afternoon both by the minister and by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), there is no question about it that the ending of this cold war and the finding of the basis for peace depend in no small measure upon the economic health of the world. We believe that this economic health must be planned more specifically than it has been planned in the past. We need effective planning to raise the standard of living everywhere. We need concrete plans to increase the productivity and means of distribution of the world and to build up particularly the economies of Asia and of Africa, as well as that of Europe, to higher levels and standards. I believe that this involves our steadfast adherence to the principles of the United Nations and its specialized agencies which deal with these particular problems.
IMr. ColdweUJ	l*MI
We are glad that in recent months and years we have seen specific steps in this direction. We have the success of the Marshall plan in rebuilding the European economy; the recent decisions of the north Atlantic nations at the conference which the minister attended, to increase their economic co-operation under article 2 of the North Atlantic agreement; the adherence of Canada and the United States to such organizations as that for European economic co-operation. Then we have the Schuman proposal to which the minister referred this afternoon. This is one of the most remarkable proposals the world has seen for generations. We have France suggesting that there be an integration of the iron resources of France and the coal resources of what was Germany, with a view to their joint development for the benefit of the whole of the European economy. How this will be done will have to be worked out in the future. I am inclined to think that the problem is a difficult one because you have the tug of war between those who believe that it should be done under various privately-owned organizations and those who believe it should be done under public ownership and organization; and governments, like that of the United Kingdom, which feel the need for public ownership, international ownership and administration, are afraid that the privately-owned set-up would result once again in a great private cartel that might even restrict production rather than expand it and thus defeat the very objective that this great Schuman plan should have in mind.
Then we have the European economic commission of the United Nations, and the other organizations that are subsidiary to the U.N., all of which are working for international co-operation and which are all to the good. No responsible political party and no responsible parliament can fail to recognize that the world today is divided into two parts. We have not hesitated to state where we stand in this matter. We stand with those forces that are determined to retain, to expand and to promote everywhere the democratic ideals of human right and of fundamental freedom. We have recognized and have stated that the cold war is due to the fact that the new imperialism-I think that is the correct description of it-of the U.S.S.R. and its ruthless exploitation of the communist parties everywhere in the European and Asiatic countries are the major threats both to democracy and to peace. We have therefore supported the Marshall plan-and are continuing to do so-the Brussels treaty and the Atlantic pact, all of which seek to unite the democratic world, both for its own defence and also-something which is part of its

defence, of course-for possible international co-operation in the economic field. That is not only the policy of this movement; incidentally it is the policy of the democratic socialist groups and parties throughout the whole of western Europe and indeed the whole of the world. At the same time,_ in common with such parties, we will continue to oppose anything that seems to be contrary to the principles of the United Nations charter and to the aims of international economic co-operation. We believe that it is equally important to stand against pressures of capitalists who would try to rebuild the world on the old plan of economic imperialism of the pre-war sort and those who want to control the world under the new type of imperialism that is promoted by the Soviet union and her satellites at the present time. We believe that the thing we must do is to join together with all democratic countries in the world in standing firmly against any infringement of freedom and democracy, from whatever quarter it may come.
We are glad indeed that the government, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs, has consistently supported the United Nations and its subsidiary organizations. We think that this country more and more should endeavour to see to it that all the positive agencies of the United Nations should be strengthened and should be used. What we want to see, of course, is the prestige of the United Nations restored at once to the extent to which it has been lost; and I think there has been a loss of prestige in the last year or two. But most of all, we want to see the prestige of the United Nations greatly increased. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) mentioned the recognition of the new government of China. That, of course, has been a matter of discussion and controversy in most democratic countries. But it seems to us that when we fail to admit that the new government of China is in power we are cutting ourselves off from four or five hundred million people in Asia.
After all, we have in the United Nations governments that are perhaps more thoroughly dominated by the communist party than is that of China. In this I find myself reinforced by the opinions of Nehru, the government of the United Kingdom, and other people throughout the world who believe that recognition under international law does not mean that recognition of a country implies approval of its government. However, if we want to maintain contact with this great country in Asia, then we should reconsider our position in respect of the new government in China and grant it recognition.
External Affairs
In passing may I observe that I believe a new attempt should be made at the forthcoming meeting of the assembly to reach an agreement on the thorny problem of atomic energy. In a speech over the radio by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) some time ago he seemed to imply that there might be some modification of the position that had been taken, and that there was hope that with some modification agreement could be reached. We have regarded it as essential that whatever is done shall include within the agreement the right of the United Nations authority engaged in atomic energy inspection to be free at all times to examine within every country any atomic energy project and, indeed, anything which may look like an atomic energy project, including the mining of the radioactive material.
I hope a new attempt will be made, because our people are greatly disturbed. Recently a petition was circulated across Canada for the banning of the bomb. In my opinion the petition was deceptive because it excluded the one vital thing, and indeed when it was first presented to me in draft form I refused to endorse it unless a clause were inserted demanding the right of unrestricted inspection in every country of the world by a United Nations commission. Without that, in my opinion the banning of the bomb or the signing of petitions of this kind would not only be ineffective but would lull us into a false sense of security. I wanted to say that, although the matter was not discussed this afternoon.
Economic co-operation must be stressed by the representatives of Canada. I know Canada has been interested in article 2 of the treaty, from the beginning. So far as those of us in this party are concerned, we have laid great stress upon it both in the house and in the country because, after all, to the extent that the nations can improve their economies, just to that extent are we strong and to that extent can we remove the causes of discontent in which some totalitarian ideology may take root and flourish. Again I use the expression "'some totalitarian ideology," because, while we may be concentrating upon the communist ideology and its totalitarianism, we must not forget that there is a real danger that, given the right conditions, we may see a revival of something resembling fascism or nazism in European and, indeed, Asiatic countries.
Consequently we need to stress that, as quickly as possible, the economic conditions of the various countries shall be greatly improved. Apart altogether from

External Affairs
the Schuman proposal of international development and control of iron and coal and steel, I believe we need to go beyond that and have some international arrangement so that transport, electricity and some of the other vital and fundamental aspects of our economic life may also be utilized and controlled socially and internationally.
The Schuman plan, in other words, is in our opinion a step in the right direction, and we support it; but it does not go far enough to meet the needs at the present time. Although I do not wish to discuss the matter in detail this afternoon, there is of course the matter of co-operation in all phases of world trade, to improve the trading relationships of countries so that, for example, they may have access to our food supplies, such as wheat, and we may have access to some of the things they produce and which we could use, such as vegetable oils, perhaps, and even raw rubber-although we have a synthetic plant. There would be numerous other commodities which, if available, would enable us to improve our standard of living. Together, then, we could guarantee higher standards and greater freedom for all mankind.
At all times Canada should encourage the forces of progress, wherever they exist, and assist everywhere in the realization of that part of the United Nations charter which calls for the recognition of human rights and fundamental freedoms. If we are going to have racial equality and religious freedom we must see to it that we have no prejudices and intolerances in our own country. In other words, example is better than precept. Every time we permit in our own country something which looks like intolerance, or the refusal to recognize certain democratic rights of association, of speech, of worship or of religion, it is used by the enemies not only of our own country but of democracy throughout the world.
We need political democracy and we need economic democracy as well. We talk about raising the standard of living, so I regret very much that some few months ago our government did not support wholeheartedly and fully the food and agriculture organization plan for distributing food to the needy people of the world. As a matter of fact in the economic and social council Canada opposed international action to maintain full employment.
I think that not only is that a mistake, but that it casts a reflection upon the good faith of our country in connection with its international efforts for a better world. Apart from the North Atlantic pact, which 
I believe, as the minister said, is an essential part of the United Nations, we should press constantly for the establishment of an international police force under the security council, so that a nation like this, or any other nation in a similar situation, may not have to expend so tremendous a proportion of its manpower, its energies, its basic resources, and what we might call its wealth, upon preparations for military defence. Indeed, those preparations for military defence may very well place in danger the very cause that we have at heart, but as long as we have no security through the security council of the United Nations we must consider ways and means of defending our own country and assisting in the defence of the group of countries with which we are associated.
I welcome the decisions that have been made over the months for the north Atlantic group of nations to co-ordinate their defence preparations, and I believe that Canada must carry out fully her obligations within these agreements and understandings; but I hope the time is not far distant when these obligations will be carried out under the aegis of the security council of the United Nations.
I was glad the minister stressed what he called the division of effort. I think those were the words he used, or they were words to that effect. Indeed this is a new form of division of labour in the world so that we and other nations can decide what we can do best. I held the view, even before the last war-sometimes I was criticized for having said it-that Canada's best contribution could be made in the realm of economic aid. I still think that, should war break out again, in all probability this country would become a greater source of economic aid than it was in the last war. We might even become the arsenal of democracy. That does not mean that we should not participate in the armed forces of the Atlantic group, but I think we should endeavour to see to it that we play our part in the most effective and efficient way that can be determined in consultation with those nations that are united with us under the Atlantic treaty.
I believe the democratic world has the physical, economic and spiritual forces to win, let us say not the war but the peace.
I have heard, with a good deal of interest, many leading statesmen of the world state, as President Truman stated only a few days ago, that war is not imminent or inevitable. Nothing is inevitable. I still believe that if we remain strong in ourselves, if we improve the standards of living of the people

across the world and strengthen the democratic institutions in this country and the democratic people with similar institutions, war may never come. That is what we should hope and pray for. But of course we should not live in a fool's paradise, believing, while we may think it is not inevitable, that we are not threatened at the present time by the expansionist demands and projects of communist totalitarianism under the Soviet union. As days go by we must be vigilant lest we find that we are threatened by the expansionist ideas of other great countries in the world. I believe that if we use the economic, physical, spiritual and moral resources that we have we can win through and with like-minded peoples maintain the peace of the world.
Then we might as a nation assist in building a world society from which war will be banished permanently and in which all the peoples of the earth may live in peace and freedom. That of course is what the minister visualized during the course of his remarks -one world. Undoubtedly the day will come when there will be just one world, but we must make sure that we are laying a foundation for a democratic and free world. When there is government at the international level, when there is a freely elected parliament of man, then we shall have achieved the age-old desire of men that war be banished from the world.
As I close, let me emphasize that I believe that that can come only when the resources of the world are used to the advantage of all the peoples of the world and when the standards of living of the world have been raised and poverty, misery, want and disease, as far as those evils are undeserved, have been banished for ever from our midst.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made this afternoon by the minister of external affairs and, as was so well said by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I look forward to the supplementary statement to be made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) following his return from a long journey to India, New Zealand and Australia. While it is in mind, may I say that I would like to have had the minister explain a little more the statements or declarations that came out of the meeting at London having to do with the relationship of the policy laid down there to Africa and the development of the colonial possessions of the various countries in that continent, which I understand has as its objective the final independence of those colonies. Naturally Canada is not very much 55946-203
External Affairs
interested in the continent of Africa, especially as far as colonies or possessions are concerned, but we do have an interest in that we will share, as a member nation in the Atlantic union, in the responsibility when action is contemplated in that country.
The trouble I usually find with the pronouncements that come out of London or ministers' conferences or Atlantic pact meetings is that they are couched in language that nobody can clearly understand. I do not know whether that is done deliberately or whether it is unavoidable, but the fact is that I find they are usually capable of many different interpretations. I wonder if the people who draft them do not expect the average citizen, and I am only one of them, to experience some preconceived emotional reaction rather than to understand some of the objectives we are really struggling to achieve.
I have been watching the press ever since the minister went to London and have been reading the pronouncements that have been made. I must confess that I was not able to make too much of some of them. I found also that the minister's statement this afternoon contained terms that were difficult for the average man to understand fully. I must confess to an occasional feeling of uneasiness about where all these international commitments are going to lead the people of Canada and finally leave us when eventually peace is attained through co-operative action. Sometimes I wonder what the language of the minister envisions. I read a speech he made while he was in London, I believe. On that occasion he spoke of the necessity of surrendering our national sovereignty, as a prerequisite to the achievement of world peace. I wonder exactly what it is that the minister wants Canada to do, and I suppose not only Canada but the other signatory nations. To my knowledge he has never made his views clear in this respect. This is the time to do it, and I think he should do so.
The people of Canada surely ought to know exactly what we are going to be expected to do with respect to the surrender of our sovereignty, our liberty as a nation. I for one am not satisfied with the rather nebulous things that have been said up to this time in that regard. There is a substantial portion of the Canadian people who, like me, wonder if those individuals who are planning the course of world events have not in their minds the final establishment of a world government to which this and all other nations will one day wake up to find that they have surrendered every effective sovereign right they ever possessed. That is the fear in the

External Affairs
minds of a good many people; and, once they are surrendered, it is mighty difficult to get them back.
I speak for all my colleagues when I caution the minister to look out. We think that Canada should be prepared to co-operate with the Atlantic community nations and other nations of the world-but of course we are speaking now more particularly of the Atlantic nations-to the fullest possible extent in any bona fide effort to bring peace and security to this old world. Canada has always conducted herself in the past in such a way that our reputation for honesty and trustworthiness is well known, and is never doubted by anyone in the whole world. That being the case, I contend it cannot be necessary for us to surrender permanently any part of our sovereignty. Our word is our bond. Our actions in the past have so often spoken for us that we should never have to put up any further security to seal our good intentions. Therefore in any integration of our economic and military strength with those of other nations we demand that every safeguard be set up so that the future will not find us short as to our right of self-determination in very important aspects.
The minister should make himself crystal clear as to what he expects Canada and other nations to do in the surrender of their sovereignty. I maintain that the American nations -and I mean all the American nations-must preserve their liberty and never be found in a position where they cannot order their own affairs as they want to order them when it becomes necessary for them to do so, as it doubtless will.
Canadians generally will be pleased to hear that the policy to be followed by the Atlantic nations is not a strategy of, as the minister said this afternoon, the liberation of European countries after occupation and destruction. If he did not use these words he at least implied that the strategy to be followed would be one of defending rather than rescuing. I am all for that, but let me point out, Mr. Speaker, that that is the spirit of the British commonwealth at its best. The British commonwealth has always held defending rather than rescuing as a tradition. That is the principle by which the British commonwealth grew and waxed strong in right and justice.
It must also be comforting for people generally to know that the nations of the north Atlantic union are showing considerable inclination to plan their defences as a team. I do not think that there is any question about the necessity for the strongest and closest possible team work. No doubt the closer and more effective the co-operation amongst these

nations the less social and economic disruption there will be within them. No people can be counted upon to do their best if they are discontent or at the point of protesting against the economic burden. The minister said in his address this afternoon that the north Atlantic nations are not concentrating merely on military preparations for strong defensive measures. That was pleasant to my ears. He declared that due regard would be had for the economic and social stability of the member nations now and in the years to come. We Social Crediters as you know, Mr. Speaker, have consistently taken the position that our contribution to the Atlantic pact, and to movements for world peace and security, cannot be very great or effective unless we keep the production of every kind of wanted material and service at a very high level. That is Why, in the course of the budget debate this year, we advocated the setting up of a commission to survey Canada's potential productive capacity in order to make sure that we are not overlooking something, to make certain exactly where we stand with respect to our policy to produce the things that we and the world need.
Not only that; we need to know to what extent we can take advantage of our capacity to produce. That is why we have constantly laid emphasis on production. We are glad to see that very important studies are going on at the national research council. There is a committee now studying the affairs of the council. Just the other day when we visited the laboratories on Sussex street we saw some things that gladdened my heart at least, and made me feel very proud of what that body is achieving. One thing that impressed me was that there are certain studies going on with respect to the ability of Canada to become self-sufficient in the production of oils and fats. It was most impressive when I saw what they were doing. I found, for example, that certain scientists are pressing forward with all their strength and ability to help Canadians to know that we have right within our boundaries the source of all the fats and oils that we need for food purposes, as well as those that are being developed in the west for industrial and home use.
I was amazed to find, for example, that we had made considerable strides towards almost self-sufficiency in cooking fats through the use of such common things as rapeseed of which we can produce an almost limitless abundance. They have even gone so far as to recover quantities of palatable and edible cooking fats from the lowly stinkweed and mustard seed that we thought hitherto were just a nuisance to man instead of being a potential blessing if we use them rightly.

There are so many other things that we are finding out, but I heard one of the scientists say, "it burns me up when I find I cannot impress people in this country with the necessity for using these things." It is easy to go out and buy when you have the wherewithal to buy. It is another thing to produce. The mark of a successful nation, of a nation full of vitality, is its ability to make use of the things that are at hand. The only way we can do that is to concentrate our attention upon the findings of the national research council and others who are engaged in investigations of that kind; then, when the information is disseminated, try to direct the minds of our industrialists and our people generally into those channels where they will believe that they should be using Canadian products in so far as they possibly can. Some day we might be called upon to fall back on our own resources, and then if we have the know-how we might be able to prevent unnecessary suffering that might result from impotence.
The minister said little about Germany. I had hoped he might be able to throw a little further light on what he was able to give us in the external affairs committee not long ago. Since he appeared before that committee I believe there have been some important developments, especially in eastern Germany. We are told now that it is known the Russians have been able to organize a fairly substantial army. They call it a secret police body, but in reality it is an army. Just how the presence of that army in eastern Germany affects the security of the people in western Germany, it seems to me ought to be given the most careful consideration. I do not know whether the minister has anything further on it; but, if he has, I for one would certainly appreciate some statement with respect to it when he speaks.
I should also like to have him give us something about the way the western nations are making headway against the determined drive by Russia to win Germany over to the Russian way of thinking; whether or not the combined communist-nationalist ory that is arising in eastern Germany is beginning to take hold in the minds of the people in western Germany. The people of Germany are susceptible to that sort of thing, and especially are they swayed by anything that has the touch of nationalism, particularly nationalism for Germany. It might be that the minister has something he could say to reassure us in that respect, but perhaps he has not.
I should like to join with the member for Rosetown-Biggar in pointing out that, when 55946-203^	|
External Affairs
the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations suggested the world pool idea for the distribution of surplus food, and then the officials of the international monetary fund were allowed to influence them against it, that division of the United Nations lost a great deal of prestige. We have argued this matter many times, but somehow or other there seems to be a disposition on the part of the officials of this country at least to support the action that was induced by the officials of the international monetary fund. The time is coming when that international pooling will prove to be an absolute necessity; it is not far ahead. I am satisfied that the officials of this country who have charge of these affairs must, sooner or later, come to see that that is the only solution to this recurring problem of surplus food materials. The sooner we get at the setting up of that organization the better it is going to be for us all. I know the minister has had little, if anything, to do with that part of our international relations, but 1 merely echo what the member for Rosetown-Biggar said in his address. It is a very important consideration in future international relations, and may well become one of the great factors upon which international peace and security will be based.
I shall conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I think Canada ought to be prepared to go all-out in its efforts to co-operate to the fullest possible extent with the Atlantic nations in* their efforts to achieve world peace and security. I will back the minister in anything he does to achieve these worthy objectives. But it seems to me that one of our most important considerations is now being neglected. I have not heard anything coming out of any of the United Nations organizations, much less the Atlantic union, to the effect that one of the things we must do, if -the nations of the world are going to get out of the present impasse and clear away the clutter and debris of the cold war, is to get back to the rule of law. That does not mean just the rule of national law or international law. It has far wider implications than that. Every single blessing that man enjoys is predicated upon a law. If the laws upon which those blessings are predicated are broken, we cannot enjoy the blessings. You can see that in every phase of our activity, our human relationships. We have had floods in our country. I am just as satisfied as I can be that fundamentally those floods that have occurred in Manitoba came as a result of a broken law:	men defying the laws of
nature, denuding the forests or ploughing up lands that ought to have been left to grass so as to restrain the run-off; that is only an

External Affairs
example. The depletion of our forests is another example of an instance where men are setting themselves up as arbiters, and are defying the natural and fundamental laws. So it is with every aspect of our endeavours with human relationship. I believe that as a nation we ought to be concentrating upon getting people to realize that until they begin to observe law, in every one of its aspects, we cannot hope to achieve world peace. I am looking forward to the day when we shall be engaged actively on a program of this kind, and I pledge the minister my support in everything he undertakes that will lead us to that goal.

It is worth our remembering also how many people who get to this country from the other side of the iron curtain escape before their time comes for going home; and of course the very existence of the curtain itself holds out some hope they believe our way of life is what we believe it is.
To revert to what the hon. member for Peace River said, it we really practise the rule of law, if we really practise racial non-discrimination-and incidentally, that appears to be one place where we have something to learn from the Russians, as I understand it-and the other things, then it may be that there is hope in that direction.
In that connection, I should like to read a word or two from an authority which you will all be interested in and will all respect. The other day Sir Alexander Cadogan, speaking to the graduating class at McGill university, had some wise words to say. He spoke about the need of our being tranquil. He spoke about the need of not giving way to excitement and nervousness. He said quite frankly that we might have many years in which to control ourselves in the same kind of tense situation that we have now. Then he said this, which I thought was most interesting, and I am reading from the Montreal Gazette of May 30:
He warned against fatalistic despair and a current danger of ''too easy and hazy optimism, of rather loose and too hopeful thinking." No early or easy solution could be expected; it might take generations to reach the goal.
Meanwhile, free nations should do all possible to provide themselves with defence against attack.
Then there is this part that I thought was particularly apposite, and particularly practical if you take the long view:
And a positive effort should be made to convert other nations to freedom and out of tyranny. "If we the free nations can put our house in order,

labour without ceasing to develop our own resources in peace, contrive that benefits are justly shared, show that our way of life can bring happiness, that freedom of belief, freedom of speech, the right to question and criticize make for material and moral progress and strength," he said, "then it may be that we shall convert others by the teaching of hard facts which cannot forever be suppressed, and that those others may refuse longer to live under the tyranny that now oppresses them."
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we are not prepared to believe that there is something in that, it is hard to go on believing anything at all; and so I put it before you.
I think I have nothing further to add except to say that I think the advice from this great diplomat who, I suggest, has had to "take it", as we say, from the Russians at numerous international conferences in a way that passes my understanding, is something that we can well consider; we may well mark his words. I add that to what I said earlier about defence, and I will close by reminding you of these words that we have heard quoted quite often, and I am going to venture to make one small change in them. You will remember the line from one of Shakespeare's historical plays: "Out of this nettle, danger, we pluck this flower, safety." Nobody now believes that there is any great safety to be plucked but we perhaps might greatly daring venture to change the line to read: Out of this nettle, danger, we pluck this flower, courage.
